title: Building a new road can make everyone’s drive slower
body: Braess’s paradox says that adding a road to a network can lengthen everyone’s journey, because each driver picks the route that is best for them, not for the group. In the textbook example, 4,000 drivers split evenly between two routes and each takes 65 minutes. Open a free shortcut between the routes and every driver is drawn onto the same two congested stretches, so the trip takes **80 minutes**, and nobody gains by switching back alone. Arthur Pigou noticed the effect in 1920; it was named after Dietrich Braess, who analysed it in 1968. It works in reverse too: when Seoul removed the Cheonggye Expressway, traffic around the city sped up.

slides.alt: A road network: Start connects to A and B, which both connect to End. Two legs take 45 minutes; the other two take the number of cars divided by 100. A dashed new road links A and B in zero minutes. Without it every trip takes 65 minutes; with it, 80.
slides.caption: Two balanced routes, then a free shortcut that everyone takes.

slides.question: Each trip takes 65 minutes on the two routes. How long does it take once the free shortcut opens?
slides.explanation: Everyone piles onto the two stretches whose delay grows with traffic, so each trip takes 80 minutes, and no single driver gains by switching back.

slides.heading: Minutes per trip for all 4,000 drivers
slides.note: The textbook network: everyone takes the shortcut, and everyone loses 15 minutes

slides.heading: Seen in the real world
items: Seoul: traffic sped up after the Cheonggye Expressway was removed
Stuttgart, 1969: jams eased only when a new road was closed again
New York, 1990: closing 42nd Street for Earth Day cut congestion

slides.heading: Why it happens
slides.text: Each driver chooses the quickest route given what everyone else is doing, a Nash equilibrium. Once the shortcut exists, giving it up alone would hand you a slower trip, so nobody does. Only a shared agreement, or closing the road, gets everyone their 15 minutes back.

slides.question: The paradox is named after Dietrich Braess. In what year did he publish his analysis?
slides.explanation: Braess published it in 1968, 48 years after Pigou first noticed the effect. Each driver’s best reply to the others, a Nash equilibrium, is what traps them all.
